title: 26yo M Acute Behavioural Disturbance
chiefComplaint: Violently agitated, incoherent, brought in restrained by police
diagnoses: Acute behavioural disturbance with sympathomimetic toxicity
background: Found running into traffic on Rama IV, shouting, undressed to the waist and apparently responding to something nobody else could see. Police restrained him prone on the roadside for approximately eight minutes before the ambulance arrived, then transported him prone and handcuffed. Friends at the scene mentioned he had taken 'ya ba' at a party and had not slept for two days. He is 82 kg and physically powerful. Nobody has checked a glucose, a temperature or an oxygen saturation, because nobody has been able to get near him.

exam.finding: Extreme agitation with apparently undiminished strength against four people, incoherent shouting, drenched in sweat, no response to verbal de-escalation. This combination of extreme agitation, hyperthermia and exhaustion is the presentation that precedes sudden cardiac arrest in custody

Pupils 7 mm and sluggish, dry mucous membranes, abrasions to the forehead and left cheek from the roadside restraint, no obvious skull deformity, no blood from the ears or nose, no neck stiffness assessable
Tachycardia at 158/min, hypertensive, warm and flushed peripheries, bounding pulses, capillary refill under 2 seconds

Tachypnoeic at 36/min with shallow ineffective breaths. Saturations 92% despite hyperventilation. Prolonged prone restraint mechanically limits chest and diaphragmatic excursion, and this is the mechanism of restraint-associated death
Soft on the limited examination possible, no distension, no guarding, no external evidence of abdominal trauma from the restraint
Hot, flushed and profusely diaphoretic. Abrasions over both wrists from handcuffs, grazes over both knees and the anterior chest from the roadside. No needle marks, no rash, no petechiae

GCS 13 but unassessable in detail because of the agitation. No lateralising weakness observed during struggling. Moving all four limbs. Any patient with an unexplained agitated delirium has a head injury and a metabolic cause until both are excluded

investigations.name: Capillary glucose
investigations.report: Low. Hypoglycaemia can present as pure aggressive agitation with no other feature, it is fully reversible in ninety seconds, and it is the single most common reversible cause missed in a patient assumed to be intoxicated or psychotic. Check it in every agitated patient before anything else.

investigations.name: Rectal core temperature
investigations.report: Hyperthermia from sustained muscle activity plus a sympathomimetic. A core temperature above 40 C in an agitated patient is an emergency in its own right and predicts rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy and arrest.

investigations.name: Venous blood gas and lactate
investigations.report: Profound mixed acidosis. Sustained maximal muscle exertion against restraint produces a lactate in this range, and when restraint also limits ventilation the respiratory compensation fails. This blood gas is the physiology of restraint death written down.

investigations.name: Creatine kinase
investigations.report: Rhabdomyolysis, rising. Will peak at 24 to 72 hours.

investigations.name: Potassium and creatinine
investigations.report: Hyperkalaemia with acute kidney injury from myoglobinuria. Combined with the acidosis this is an arrhythmogenic state.

investigations.name: 12-Lead ECG (once sedated)
investigations.report: Sinus tachycardia at 152/min with peaked T waves and a QRS of 118 ms from hyperkalaemia and acidosis. No ST elevation. QTc 470 ms.

investigations.name: CT brain (once sedated and stable)
investigations.report: No intracranial haemorrhage, no contusion, no skull fracture despite the facial abrasions. Normal. Obtained because the history of head contact during restraint could not be excluded clinically.

data.label: Get him off his front, immediately and before anything else
actions: Remove from prone position, turn supine or lateral
Remove pressure from the back and chest
Uncuff the hands from behind the back

doseMap.Remove from prone position, turn supine: Prone restraint with weight on the back is the mechanism of restraint-associated death: it prevents chest expansion in a patient with a massive oxygen debt. No patient should be left prone for a moment longer than it takes to control the limbs

data.label: Rapid chemical sedation, because physical restraint is what is killing him
actions: Or midazolam plus droperidol IM if ketamine is unavailable
Prepare airway equipment before giving it

doseMap.Ketamine IM: 4-5 mg/kg IM (about 350 mg) for severe agitation. Onset 3-5 minutes, preserves airway reflexes and respiratory drive, and does not drop the blood pressure. It is the agent of choice when the priority is stopping the muscle activity fast
doseMap.Or midazolam plus droperidol IM if ketam: Midazolam 5-10 mg IM with droperidol 10 mg IM. Slower onset and more respiratory depression
doseMap.Prepare airway equipment before giving i: Have suction, bag-valve-mask and intubation drugs at the bedside. A proportion of patients given dissociative doses of ketamine need airway support, and laryngospasm is uncommon but real

data.label: The moment he is sedated, treat this as a medical emergency and not a behavioural one

doseMap.Capillary glucose: Ninety seconds, and it is the diagnosis in a meaningful minority of these patients. Sedating an agitated hypoglycaemic patient without treating the glucose is how people die in cubicles
doseMap.Dextrose for hypoglycaemia: 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV, recheck at 30 minutes

data.label: Aggressive cooling and fluid resuscitation
actions: Calcium gluconate for the hyperkalaemic ECG changes

doseMap.Active cooling to below 38.5 C: Ice packs to neck, axillae and groin with misting and fanning. As in heat stroke, antipyretics do not work here because the set point is normal
doseMap.Large volume crystalloid: 2 litres initially, then target urine output 2 mL/kg/h for the rhabdomyolysis

data.label: Physiology begins to correct
data.narrative: Muscle activity stops within four minutes of ketamine. Over the next hour temperature falls to 38.6 C, lactate to 6.2 and pH rises to 7.24. He requires airway support with a nasopharyngeal airway and a jaw thrust but not intubation. Stopping the muscle activity was the treatment for the acidosis, the hyperthermia and the hyperkalaemia simultaneously.

data.label: Document the restraint honestly and speak to him afterwards as a patient (Empathy)
data.narrative: You write down the eight minutes of prone restraint, the transport position, and the fact that no glucose or temperature was obtained before arrival. Not as an accusation, as a fact with a time next to it. Then, on day two when he is lucid and ashamed and expecting to be spoken to like a problem, you tell him what actually happened to his body, that he came close to dying of it, and that this is a medical condition with treatment rather than a character verdict. He asks for the drug service referral himself. Pi Pim uses the case in teaching and the ambulance service changes its transport position policy nine months later.

data.label: Exclude the organic causes you could not exclude while he was fighting
actions: Full septic screen if fever persists after cooling
Serial creatine kinase and renal function

doseMap.Full septic screen if fever persists aft: Do not attribute everything to the stimulant. Meningoencephalitis presents as agitated delirium and the diagnosis is made by the person who keeps asking after the obvious answer is available

data.label: Course
data.narrative: Creatine kinase peaks at 31000 on day 2. Creatinine peaks at 3.2 mg/dL with good urine output on aggressive fluids, and he avoids dialysis. Awake and orientated by 14 hours. CT brain and CSF both normal.

data.label: Disposition
data.narrative: Discharged day 5 with normal renal function, a psychiatric review that found no primary psychotic illness, and an accepted referral to substance use services. The two decisions that mattered were turning him off his front in the first thirty seconds and checking a glucose before assuming the diagnosis was written on the ambulance sheet.
